notes.trap: If the value is not found and the array contains a NULL element, the result is NULL, not false. This NULL is easy to miss inside WHERE or NOT filters.
The index is 1-based and returned as BIGINT. A missing element gives 0, not NULL as in some other engines, so `IS NULL` checks never fire.
`get(...)` is 0-based, unlike `element_at(...)` and `array_position(...)`, which are 1-based. Out-of-range and negative indexes return NULL even with ANSI on.
In Spark 3.5, index -1 inserts after the last element. In 3.4 it inserted before the last element. An index past the end pads the array with NULLs, and index 0 raises an error.
Without the third nullReplacement argument, NULL elements are dropped silently, with no empty slot or doubled delimiter. Positional meaning is lost.
NaN counts as greater than every non-NaN double or float, so a single NaN makes it the maximum. NULL elements are skipped.
If there is no common non-null element, both arrays are non-empty and either one contains a NULL, the result is NULL instead of false.
It cannot remove NULLs. Passing NULL as the element makes the whole result NULL. Use `array_compact(...)` to drop NULL elements.
The result is set-like: duplicates in the first array are removed even when they do not appear in the second array.
Stop is inclusive. With no step, the step defaults to -1 when start > stop, so a reversed range gives a descending array rather than an empty one.
If any inner array is NULL, the whole result is NULL. The NULL inner array is not skipped.
Arrays of different lengths are not truncated to the shortest. The result has the length of the longest array, and missing fields are filled with NULL.
With ANSI off, mixed element types are coerced to a common wider type. A number mixed with a string silently produces an array of strings.
A negative count returns an empty array, not an error. A NULL count returns NULL.
